**Status: preliminary (v0).** Scope is PSE's retail load in Kitsap County, the system KPUD would acquire. Every input is labeled; see the provenance table at the end. All values are ESTIMATES unless stated otherwise.

## Headline

| Quantity (2025) | Low | Central | High | Stress range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Annual retail energy (TWh) | 1.74 | 2.04 | 2.60 | 1.52–2.66 |
| Average load at meter (MW) | 199 | 233 | 297 | 173–303 |
| Average load incl. losses (MW) | 206 | 242 | 315 | |
| Annual peak (MW) | 342 | 471 | 738 | |

- FindEnergy's **3.24 TWh** (and the ~370 MW average it implies) is not a measurement of Kitsap. It is Washington's statewide per-capita use (11.66 MWh) times county population (Method A). It is **1.58x** this module's central estimate and 22% above even the stress-high case.
- KUOW's "around 370 megawatts" (UNVERIFIED, S016) does not say average or peak. As an **average** it is 1.59x the central estimate and above even the stress-high case. As a **peak** it falls inside this module's peak range (342–738 MW). It fits a peak figure. It does not fit average energy.
- Peak demand is the least certain number here. It drives substation, transmission and BPA capacity costs, so PSE's Kitsap-area peak data is the top data request (OQ-05).

## Method A: FindEnergy county figure (tested, not used)

- FindEnergy Kitsap: 3,236,601 MWh / population 277,673 = **11.656 MWh per person**.
- FindEnergy Washington statewide: **11.66 MWh per person** (90,752,364 MWh). The same value appears on the Kittitas and Jefferson pages (S014).
- Statewide per-capita x Kitsap population = 3,237,667 MWh, matching the published figure. Verdict: **statewide average scaled by population**. The statewide average includes data-center, pulp-and-paper and irrigation loads Kitsap does not have. Even a correct county total would also include BPA's federal direct-service load (S013) and Peninsula Light and Mason PUD 3 customers, none of which KPUD would acquire from PSE.

## Method B: back-calculated from the 2022 county GHG inventory

kWh = (electricity tCO2e, S006) / (PSE carbon intensity, S007–S009). The inventory publishes emissions, not kWh, and does not say which PSE factor it used. Every plausible factor:

| Fuel-mix year | CI component | PSE factor (gCO2e/MJ) | Implied 2022 total (TWh) | Implied location-based factor (lb/MWh) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | lifecycle total | 135.03 | 1.70 | 284 |
| 2021 | production-to-consumption | 119.78 | 1.92 | 252 |
| 2022 | lifecycle total | 122.59 | 1.88 | 258 |
| 2022 | production-to-consumption | 109.25 | 2.11 | 230 |
| 2023 | lifecycle total | 102.08 | 2.25 | 215 |
| 2023 | production-to-consumption | 90.29 | 2.55 | 190 |

Cases used (low/high = the largest/smallest factor in the matrix; central = 2022 mix, production-to-consumption. It matches the inventory year, it is the component that includes T&D, and community inventories normally exclude upstream emissions):

| Load case | PSE factor (gCO2e/MJ) | tCO2e/MWh | Residential (MWh) | Commercial (MWh) | Industrial (MWh) | Total 2022 (TWh) | Total 2025 pop-scaled (TWh) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| low | 135.03 | 0.4861 | 1,176,405 | 521,448 | 6,163 | 1.70 | 1.74 |
| central | 109.25 | 0.3933 | 1,454,005 | 644,495 | 7,618 | 2.11 | 2.15 |
| high | 90.29 | 0.3250 | 1,759,331 | 779,833 | 9,217 | 2.55 | 2.60 |

- Sector split (all cases): residential 69.0%, commercial 30.6%, industrial 0.4%. This holds only if one emission factor was applied to every sector (OQ-02).
- Population scaling 2022 to 2025: x1.0219 (OFM, S006), with per-customer use held flat.

**eGRID cross-check.** The inventory also reports a location-based figure (219,570 tCO2e) using an unnamed "regional" eGRID factor. Dividing by each published eGRID2022 rate (S023):

| eGRID basis | Rate (lb CO2e/MWh) | Implied total (TWh) | PSE factor that total would require (gCO2e/MJ) |
|---|---|---|---|
| NWPP subregion | 605.9 | 0.80 | 288.0 |
| NWPP incl. grid gross loss | 638.5 | 0.76 | 303.5 |
| Washington state | 186.0 | 2.60 | 88.4 |
| Washington state incl. NWPP gross loss | 196.0 | 2.47 | 93.2 |

- The NWPP subregion rate implies a PSE factor about twice anything Ecology has published for PSE (90–135), so the inventory probably did not apply NWPP to the same kWh.
- The Washington state rate implies ~2.5–2.6 TWh, near the top of the matrix (2023-mix production-to-consumption). The check leans toward the upper half of Method B's range but cannot settle it. The consultant's actual factors are records request item 4.

Low and high are the corner combinations giving the minimum and maximum total (every input at its worst end at once), so this is a deliberately wide stress range.

|---|---|---|---|---|

- Method C central (1.94 TWh) is -10.0% from Method B central (2.15 TWh). The two share no inputs except the <1% industrial uplift. Method B's whole range sits inside Method C's stress range.

## Peak demand

Peak = retail / (1 − loss fraction) / 8,760 / load factor. Low-load cases pair with low losses and a high load factor, and high-load cases with the reverse.

| Case | Retail (TWh) | Loss fraction | Avg MW incl. losses | Load factor | Peak (MW) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| low | 1.74 | 0.0350 | 206 | 0.6028 | 342 |
| central | 2.04 | 0.0374 | 242 | 0.5148 | 471 |
| high | 2.60 | 0.0557 | 315 | 0.4268 | 738 |

Load factors are from 2025 observed peaks (EIA-861), not 1-in-10 cold-weather design peaks. A planning peak would be higher.

## Monthly shape (central case)

Class shares are PSE system-wide billed sales averaged over 2022–2025 (EIA-861M, S011). Billing lag shifts the shape by roughly half a month. Kitsap probably peaks harder in winter than PSE's system as a whole, since more of its homes heat with electricity.

## Projections

Customers grow with the OFM population projection. Per-customer use changes linearly to its 2045 value. EV energy is added above the 2026 registered fleet. The load factor is held constant, which is a simplification: heat pumps raise winter peaks and managed EV charging can lower them.
